========================================
Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring - Published Russia has launched the largest attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the spring, primarily targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, Ukraine's Prime Minister has said. At least five people were killed in overnight attacks across the country, including a child in the Kyiv region, Serhiy Koretskyi said. The strikes also impacted people's power supplies, with Ukraine's biggest private energy firm DTEK saying power to 8,000 homes had been restored following "a difficult night" for the capital. The Russian defence ministry said one of its targets was the Trypilska power station, the largest supplier of electricity to Kyiv. The operator confirmed damage to the plant. Koretskyi wrote on Telegram: "Since the summer, there has effectively not been a single day without enemy attacks on our energy infrastructure. "However, a mass and combined attack of this scale has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season." Ukraine has been expecting another protracted Russian assault on the country's energy grid. It has happened every winter so far since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022. In total, 11 regions of the country were attacked overnight, with residential buildings, social infrastructure, civilian enterprises and railways also targeted, Koretskyi said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said there had been strikes on critical infrastructure in the Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, Kirovohrad and Rivne regions. On Wednesday, some households in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Sumy and Kharkiv regions remained without power, Ukraine's energy ministry said. State-owned grid operator Ukrenergo advised residents not to use powerful electrical appliances between the hours of 10:00 and 16:00 local time as electricity supplies were lower than usual. In Kyiv, people woke to find the city blanketed by thick, acrid smoke after a night punctuated by the sound of explosions. An air raid alert was still on and the distant sound of air defence gunfire echoed through the murky atmosphere. Residents in several districts were advised to close their windows until the smoke cleared. Among those killed in the overnight strikes was a child whose body was found under the rubble of a house, Kyiv regional head Timur Tkachenko said. Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klischko said three people were killed in total in the capital, including a Ukrainian utility company worker who was killed at a warehouse building. Another person was killed in the southern Mykolaiv region, acting regional head Heorhiy Reshetilov said. Two more people were killed in the north-eastern Sumy region on Tuesday, regional head Oleh Hryhorov said. A school was also hit there in a separate strike, he added. Russia's defence ministry said it had launched massive overnight strikes on Ukrainian facilities. It said targets included the Trypilska thermal power plant, located some 40km from Kyiv, and claimed the plant supplied electricity to Ukrainian defence facilities. The operator of the plant, Centrenergo, said it was assessing the scale of the damage. Russia's military added that it had intercepted more than 380 Ukrainian drones overnight over a number of regions, including Moscow. Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said it had struck a number of Russian military targets, including a drone warehouse in the occupied Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine. Russia currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including a large area of Donetsk. On the battlefield, Ukraine's Third Army Corps said it had recaptured several settlements near the city of Lyman in Donetsk this week, as part of a counter-offensive called Operation Vivaldi. Zelensky visited troops in the area on Wednesday. But elsewhere, the front line remains largely stagnant, with both sides failing to make significant gains. Related topics - Published20 September

item.title: Last UK and US troops leave Iraq as anti-Islamic State mission ends
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65ym1dyn92mo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Last UK and US troops leave Iraq as anti-Islamic State mission ends - Published The last British and American troops have left Iraq after a military presence of more than a decade in the country. The exit of the remaining UK military personnel - around 100 - from Irbil, in the northern Kurdistan region, was co-ordinated over recent weeks with US forces, who also departed on Wednesday. It follows an agreement between the US and the Iraqi government, signed two years ago, to withdraw foreign troops by the end of this month. British and US forces have been present in Iraq since 2014, as part of the international coalition to help defeat the extremist Islamic State (IS) group. Their departure brings the mission, known as Operation Inherent Resolve, to an end. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the end of the coalition's mission marked "Iraq's transition to a phase in which it assumes full responsibility for its security and stability". Iraq is set to hold four "Sovereignty Days" as a national holiday to mark the withdrawal. "Following more than a decade of operations, training and capacity building, Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) and the Kurdish Peshmerga have secured the enduring territorial defeat of Daesh in Iraq and are now well placed to take primary responsibility for the country's security," the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in a statement, referring to IS by an Arabic acronym. "With these objectives achieved, Iraq and its international partners can begin a new chapter focused on enduring security co-operation under Iraqi leadership." US President Donald Trump celebrated the withdrawal, calling it a "victory for the United States, a victory for Iraq, and a decisive victory over ISIS". Writing in a Truth Social post, the president added: "It has been a long time, with very bad decision-making that got us involved in this quagmire in the first place, but soon, that will be part of History." Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell also said the coalition's departure from Irbil marked "the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated [IS] in Iraq". He added: "The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including [IS] remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the government of Iraq." The Iraqi government declared the military defeat of IS in 2017, but coalition forces remained to help prevent the group's resurgence. A recent UN report assessed that sustained counter-terrorism pressure by Iraqi security forces had left IS with several hundred fighters who were "able to carry out unsophisticated operations only". The Iraqi government also faces the challenge of Iranian-backed militias in the country. Zaidi, who took office in May, has vowed to disarm them and bring all weapons under state control following the coalition's exit. But several powerful factions have resisted his plans and could now see their influence grow without the US presence. Since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran earlier this year, militias have been targeting the remaining US and UK forces stationed at Irbil air base. Hundreds of Nato troops stationed in Baghdad left the country in March as tensions rose. A BBC team visited the coalition base in Irbil in April this year, during a fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran. They were forced to circle the base in an RAF transport aircraft while drones were being launched nearby. At the height of the US bombing campaign against Iran, the coalition base was being targeted by up to 28 drones and missiles a day. RAF Regiment Gunners, who were among the last British military personnel stationed there, had shot down more than 100 drones in the first six weeks of the war. Many of the attack drones were being launched by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. On Wednesday, signalling the end of the mission, the MoD paid tribute to UK personnel who had contributed to the counter-IS mission. It said they had provided "valuable support, training and assistance" to more than 111,000 members of the Iraqi Security Forces, including more than 21,000 Peshmerga forces in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region. It also said the RAF had conducted thousands of sorties, striking more than 2,300 IS targets. The RAF is expected to continue flying missions over neighbouring Syria, to prevent the remnants of IS from gaining a foothold. The Pentagon said the US would continue to provide "targeted training and intelligence support" to its Iraqi partners. US Central Command said the coalition's joint taskforce remained operational and was now based in Jordan. US forces will also continue their mission against IS in Syria, where the UN estimates that the group has up to 3,000 fighters. This is the third time US and UK forces have withdrawn from Iraq. Tens of thousands of US and British troops were deployed to the country in 1991 following Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait. They returned to Iraq in 2003, when US President George W Bush ordered Operation Iraqi Freedom to remove the dictator from power and eliminate weapons of mass destruction that turned out not to exist. The fierce sectarian insurgency that engulfed Iraq following the invasion cost tens of thousands of lives, including those of nearly 4,500 US military personnel and 179 British military personnel. US and UK forces left Iraq in 2011, only to return three years later, when IS threatened to take control of the country.

item.title: Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians, medic tells the BBC
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6grveejg1e2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians, medic tells the BBC - Published At least 52 civilians have been killed during three days of heavy fighting around Alamata in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, hospital sources have told the BBC. It appears government troops have taken control of the town from regional fighters and intend to push north towards Mekelle, the region's main city. Social media clips show army tanks on Alamata's streets. Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, with both accusing each other of violating a 2022 deal that ended a two-year civil war. Fighting has also affected neighbouring regions with 33 tourists stranded for the last week in Lalibela, a Unesco world heritage site. "We have heard fighting, gunfire and artillery cannons firing throughout the week," a British tourist, who asked not to be named, told the BBC's Newsday programme about clashes near Lalibela in the Amhara region. He said there was a large military presence in Lalibela, famous for being home to 13th Century churches hewn from rock and a holy site for millions of Orthodox Christians. Most visitors to the tourist hub had been unable to leave since the airport closed to commercial flights last Wednesday, though he said 14 Israeli tourists had been evacuated by military helicopter on Monday. The fighting around Lalibela has involved the army and an Amhara militia that has allied with Tigrayan fighters. Earlier in September, they joined forces with other Ethiopian armed movements to form a seven-member alliance with the stated intention of removing the government in the capital, Addis Ababa. There is also a fear that neighbouring Eritrea could be drawn into the conflict - as the government accuses Asmara of supporting the armed groups, something it denies. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas and it is difficult to find out what is happening because communications to the region have been cut. The two sides disagree over who started the latest fighting. - Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray? - Published5 days ago - WATCH: Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces? - Published2 days ago The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region. TPLF fighters are also fighting in the Afar region, in a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports. Over the last few days, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said more than 700 wounded people had been admitted to hospitals it supports in Tigray. The doctor at Alamata General Hospital, who requested anonymity, told the BBC the fighting in and around the town had taken place between Saturday and Monday, and involved heavy explosives and artillery, some of which landed in residential homes. Those killed in the crossfire included children as young as three days old, mothers and cattle herders. Twelve people had died in a single strike on the town's marketplace, the medic said. Since the fighting erupted, banking services in Tigray have been suspended by the government. Access to the internet has also been cut - though it is not clear who ordered the closure. A separate source in Alamata told the BBC there was a worsening humanitarian crisis in the area, as the town swelled with people fleeing fighting. "All the residents of the surrounding areas entered the town of Alamata by walking on foot for as long as an hour, hoping the town would be safe. "Unfortunately, everything is blocked - no banking service, no money transfer, no power, no internet, no phone. Hence people are in crisis, simply suffering, everyone is desperate and frustrated." The British tourist in Lalibela said online banking was working in Lalibela but there was a shortage of physical cash. He said the situation around the town had calmed down in the last two days and there were indications the airport, which was still being used by the military, might reopen on Thursday. "The local people, they are still scared of what might happen. The military presence here in the town has remained and a larger military force has been seen leaving the town heading north," he said. When the airport was first closed, 53 tourists had been in the town, he explained. But some had since been evacuated, including the 14 Israelis airlifted out on Monday while another five had left the day before via an NGO convoy, despite advice not to travel by road. Of the remaining tourists in Lalibela, the largest group were Americans, with Israelis, Britons, South Korean, South Africans, an Ethiopian-New Zealander and a Mexican also stranded, he said. Meanwhile, for those cut off in Tigray because of the telecoms shutdown, the Tigray Broadcasting Service (TBS), based in Addis Ababa, has started an initiative to help reconnect families. The broadcaster has said it will collect video messages via its Telegram channel from people outside the region and air them via satellite TV. While limited to greetings and updates, this will provide a rare lifeline for families separated by the blackout. The clampdown on Tigray's banking services is also affecting Tigrayans who are not physically in the region. Customers have told the BBC that bank accounts opened in Tigray have been frozen or restricted. "I boarded public transport from Addis Ababa to Adama and tried to pay using a mobile transfer, but it didn't work," said a former Mekelle resident who moved to the capital two months ago because of growing tensions in Tigray. "It has created havoc for many people like me who escaped the situation in Tigray," he told the BBC's Tigrinya service. "Many Tigrayans are now in trouble." Girl has multiple surgeries to control infections after strike in Gaza Six-year-old Raseel al-Balawi in Gaza has had more than 20 surgeries since an Israeli air strike injured her in late July. item.title: Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmrergq3j7lgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons - Published Chinese AI developer Moonshot is conducting an internal review after researchers were able to persuade two of its popular Kimi models to tell them how to make biological weapons and carry out assassinations. Mindgard, which tests the security of AI systems, told the BBC it discovered in July that Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm could evade safety limits put in place by developers. It arose during a process called "jailbreaking", where researchers use a series of complex instructions to see if AI tools ignore guardrails - which Mindgard said should have stopped Kimi from discussing concerning topics. Moonshot told the BBC it welcomed third-party input "as a key pillar for building better and safer AI". The company also told the BBC it was in discussion with Mindgard about its findings. Mindgard's founder Peter Garraghan told the BBC World Service programme Tech Life that its findings about Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm were concerning. "Once the jailbreak works it will talk about any topic, it will even freely offer up recommendations about other topics that are also nefarious and it will be inventive and creative," he said. Jailbreaks present a different kind of risk to those seen with the recent slew of high-profile AI incidents. These have seen autonomous AI tools known as agents, developed by US firms including OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic, hack some online services. While jailbreaks are complex processes that can take a lot of time and determination some experts fear hackers and other bad actors could try to use them to cause harm. Anthropic recently said it had identified and disrupted attempts to use one of its AI model for "malicious activity" that could support the development of biological weapons. Cyber-attack launchpad Mindgard has not proven whether the answers supplied by Kimi on concerning topics would work. But it argued guardrails should have prevented the models in question from entering into discussion with users on such subjects. The firm said it was also confident a jailbroken Kimi 2.6 could allow hackers to run code on its computing resources and connect to the internet - making it a potential launchpad for cyber-attacks. Garraghan defended Mindgard's decision to publicly discuss its jailbreak of Moonshot's systems, saying it had informed the developer and was not revealing key details about how it got the firm's models to ignore guardrails. Mindgard alerted Moonshot to the jailbreak in an email on 27 July, following up about a week later. It then published a blog about the issue on 12 September. But the company said Moonshot only made contact recently, after it was approached by the BBC for comment. In part of an email to Mindgard asking for more details, shared with the BBC by Moonshot, it said its model had generally shown "a high refusal rate for these types of requests" in internal evaluations. - What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it? - Published14 September Preventing jailbreaks The findings come as the AI industry continues to be split on whether closed, proprietary models - like those powering ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude systems - or open-source tools are the best or safest way forward. Kimi is an open-weight model, meaning someone could in theory take the model and run it themselves on their own computing infrastructure. Prof Alan Woodward, of the University of Surrey, told the BBC there was a risk open-source models might end up in the wrong hands, but they could also be harnessed for cyber-defence. He noted that AI firm Hugging Face used a Chinese open-source model to understand a hack later revealed to have been carried out by OpenAI agents. Prof Woodward said international regulation was unlikely to match the pace of AI development, saying: "It's taken us decades to agree on the format of telephone numbers." Like Mindgard founder Garraghan, Prof Woodward believes there should be a greater focus on identifying and prosecuting humans who misuse AI. item.title: Singapore launches matchmaking service for government workers
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqzjzr893yv4o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Singapore launches matchmaking service for government workers - Published Singapore has rolled out a matchmaking service for its government workers, an initiative that comes as the country wrestles with a record-low fertility rate. FirstDate, which launched this week for those aged 21 to 35, boasts "a different approach to dating", where it uses a Nobel-winning algorithm to match participants to one date at a time. "Swipe fatigue ends here," its website reads. Participants sign in using the national digital identity system and answer a survey about their interests, habits and values. FirstDate's launch drew mixed responses among Singaporeans, with some describing it as "dystopian" and others saying they would be keen to give it a shot. On its website, FirstDate highlights the Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage algorithm which powers the programme. The mathematical framework pairs two equally sized groups of people based on their preferences. The late mathematician Lloyd Shapley was awarded the 2012 Nobel memorial prize in economic sciences for discovering the algorithm, which has been used in public school admissions, medical residency matching, and dating apps, among other things. "At the end of the day, I think the experience of meeting someone through an application doesn't change much across the [different types of] applications," Elizabeth, a 29-year-old who works in Singapore's defence ministry and is keen on trying FirstDate out told the BBC. "But it is nice to know that the likelihood of being scammed is much lower. We're all public servants looking for a partner, right?" But some social media users say the initiative, which is currently in its pilot phase, discriminates against those not working in government. Others criticised the age limit. "They are only doing this to raise the total fertility rate. They don't actually [care] about whether we find a partner otherwise. "Since there are higher risks involved in having kids at 35 and older, the government just writes [the older singles] off," wrote another Reddit user. It is not clear if the pilot programme will be available to the wider public in future. The BBC has reached out to GovTech, the statutory board behind the pilot, for comment. The pilot launch comes as Singapore's birth rate has slumped to historic lows. For the first time in the past 60 years, fewer than 30,000 babies were born in 2025. The number of deaths meanwhile have been rising steadily in the greying nation, hitting about 26,500 in 2025. In August, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a series of new measures to better support families and to encourage couples to have children, including almost S$70,000 ($54,000; £41,000) in financial support for every child by the time they turn 17. FirstDate is not the first time the citystate is trying to play Cupid to its citizens. In 1984, it set up the Social Development Unit (SDU) tasked with organising social events to encourage graduate singles to mingle. Its exclusive target audience of university graduates was criticised as being elitist, but authorities justified the approach saying non-graduates did not seem to have difficulty finding partners. The SDU was eventually phased out. The next year, the government set up another agency to promote marriages among non-graduates. The idea of a government-run dating service is not unique to Singapore. In September 2024, Tokyo's metropolitan government launched an AI-powered dating app in an effort to combat the country's declining birth rate. The app, which is open to single residents in the city, resulted in 265 couples getting married, according to government data released in July this year. Additional reporting by Osmond Chia in Singapore

item.title: Africa's richest man launches Kenya oil refinery despite land protests
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmkg8dpwy25po?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Africa's richest man launches Kenya oil refinery despite land protests - Published Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote and Kenya's President William Ruto have broken ground on a $16bn (£12bn) oil refinery in Lamu, on Kenya's northern coast. Upon completion, the refinery is expected to process 700,000 barrels of crude oil a day, making it East Africa's largest industrial project by capacity. Ahead of the launch, some local residents took to the streets to demand more compensation for land used for the refinery. Speaking to the BBC, Dangote, Africa's richest man, dismissed the protests as games played by local marketers and international players, insisting the refinery would go ahead and would be ready by 2030 as planned. The ground-breaking was also attended by the leaders of Uganda, Ethiopia, Togo and Benin. Dangote has offered regional governments a combined 30% stake in the refinery, according to Reuters news agency. "This is Africa coming together to build Africa. Today we are not simply breaking ground for a refinery, we're breaking ground for a new chapter in Africa's industrial journey to a brighter future," Dangote said as he launched the project. "Lekki [his Nigerian refinery] proved that it can be done, Lamu must prove that it can be repeated." President Ruto made a similar point, saying: "It is a declaration that Africa has entered a new age in which we will increasingly finance, build, process and add value here at home." The refinery is set to become the only one in East Africa and is Kenya's largest infrastructure project since independence, surpassing the $5.1bn (£3.9bn) Standard Gauge Railway. In his interview with the BBC's Focus on Africa programme, Dangote disputed the compensation claims and said the company took only the portion of land it needed from what the government made available. "To come and say some people are demonstrating, demonstrating about what? Have you ever seen people demonstrating against themselves in terms of development?" he asked, indicating he was not fazed by the protests. Walid Ali, the co-founder of the Save Lamu campaign group, told the BBC that they are concerned about the environmental impact the project could have on the local community. "We are asking for the findings from the environmental impact assessment so that we can see what mitigation measures are being proposed," Ali said. "This is not the first project where we have seen environmental concerns being overlooked," he added. A group of 133 Lamu residents has approached Kenya's High Court in a bid to stop the construction work. As a result, activities such as excavation and construction on the disputed land are restricted until the next court hearing on 14 October. At the height of construction, Dangote said the refinery would create 60,000 jobs, with the benefits extending beyond those employed directly by the project. "Are we going to bring robots? Of course, the people will benefit," he said. Critics have questioned the decision to build the refinery in Kenya, which is not an oil-producing country. Others have suggested Tanzania or Uganda, both of which are moving towards oil exports through the East African Crude Oil Pipeline. But Kenya's Energy and Petroleum Minister Opiyo Wandayi told the BBC that the refinery's location did not mean it would rely on oil from the region. "Refineries get crude oil from the market. And the market is open," he said. Dangote made a similar point, citing Singapore as an example. "Singapore doesn't produce a single drop of oil, yet they have a lot of refineries," Dangote said. The refinery will also include a 1,000-megawatt power plant. Dangote sees reliable electricity as a critical constraint on industrialisation across Africa, particularly in mineral-rich countries that still export raw materials rather than processing them locally. He has about $50bn (£38bn) worth of projects in the pipeline, including plans to develop 10,000 megawatts of power generation capacity across Africa by 2030, with the potential to double that depending on demand. In Lamu, the new power plant is designed to support Dangote's operations as well as other industries expected to set up in the area. "The power is there and what you do is what we call plug and play," he said. Kenya has relatively high fuel prices, raising expectations that greater refining capacity could eventually help bring down pump prices. However, the price of crude oil, the main raw material for fuel, set by international markets, remains a major factor in what consumers pay at the pump. The Lamu refinery is Dangote's largest proposed investment outside Nigeria. His refinery in Nigeria also has a processing capacity of 700,000 barrels a day. Dangote plans to double that capacity after floating 4.1 million ordinary shares to raise up to $2.1bn earlier this month. item.title: 'He will never walk free': Indian judge's letter promises child sex abuse survivor
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq7832kn4252o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'He will never walk free': Indian judge's letter promises child sex abuse survivor - Published An Indian judge's moving letter praising a child rape survivor for her "courage" and assuring her that her abuser "will live in a cage for the rest of his life" is winning hearts in India. Trial court Judge Rajani Ranga's letter addresses the 10-year-old, who was sexually abused on 23rd July 2023 when she was seven, as "Dear child" and describes her as "the bravest little girl this court has ever seen". The trial court gave the convict a life sentence, emphasising that he would remain in prison for "the remainder of his natural life" and also awarded the survivor a compensation of 1.05m rupees ($10,941; £8,274). At the end of her order, Judge Ranga said she "must address the child victim - not in the formal language of a judgment but as a judge who has heard her voice, who has read her words, and who has been moved by her courage". "When you said 'Jab tak uncle buddhe na ho jaaye, tab tak unhe jail mein hi rakha jaaye [Keep the 'uncle' in jail until he grows old], this court listened. And this court has answered your plea," she wrote to the child survivor. "Today, this court has ordered that the man you called 'uncle' will never walk free again. He will live in a cage for the rest of his life. He will grow old in that cage. He will die in that cage. He will never be able to hurt you, or your little sister, or any other child, ever again," she added. Calling her "the bravest little girl", the judge praised her "for coming to court, pointing out the man who hurt her and telling the truth". "The man you called 'uncle' did a very bad thing to you. But you did not stay quiet. You told your mother. And because you had the courage to speak, he will never be able to hurt another child again. "The court can promise you that he will never see the sun as a free man again." Concluding her letter, the judge said the "court cannot give you back your childhood", but advised her to "now live your life. Go to school. Make friends. Laugh. Play. Dream. This court will always remember your courage". Judge Ranga's letter is part of the order that was announced on 11 July, but as cases of child sexual assault are tried in special Pocso (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences) courts, their judgments are never made public to protect the identities of the victims. It came to light after it was reproduced recently in a Delhi high court order which rejected the convict's appeal for bail and suspension of sentence. The high court order named the convict, who is an adult, but gave no other details about him. Describing Judge Ranga's letter as "a message of encouragement" to the child, the high court judges ordered the Delhi State Legal Authority to print out a copy and give it to the child along with the compensation money. The emotional letter has moved many Indians who have shared it on social media, describing it as "a rarity" and "a ray of hope" and praising the judge. Many have also expressed sorrow at the horrific nature of the crime where a child was sexually abused when she was just seven. The judge's letter may be rare, but campaigners say the seven-year-old child's case is not a rarity - more than 69,000 Pocso cases were recorded in India in 2024 alone, according to government crime data, external. And studies reveal that as in a majority of cases, abusers are known to the victims and are often trusted persons and care-givers, many cases are not even reported to the authorities. Survivors say such abuse can scar them forever and affect their entire life. In her order, Judge Ranga also addressed the issue of how such an assault can have a permanent impact on a child. After "evaluating the nature of the crime, the depth of suffering, and the lifelong impact on the victim child", she said her order was "an attempt to heal and restore" the child.

item.title: Botswana condemned for slaughtering 23 elephants for independence celebrations
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxm2qmpy57ggo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Botswana condemned for slaughtering 23 elephants for independence celebrations - Published Animal rights activists have criticised Botswana's decision to authorise the killing of 23 elephants to provide meat for independence celebrations. The southern African country, home to the world's largest elephant population, is holding nationwide festivities on Wednesday to mark the 60th anniversary of independence from Britain. A licence issued by the Ministry of Environment and Tourism, seen by local media, authorises the hunting of 23 elephants and other wild animals for "complimentary purposes". The Botswana-based Elephant Protection Society warns the decision could undermine conservation, with its chairman Oaitse Nawa telling the BBC elephants needed greater protection. He warned that slaughtering elephants for celebratory feasting could encourage poaching by creating the impression that killing elephants is acceptable when sanctioned by government. "Elephants have lost their social structures because they are always being pushed from one place to another by gunshots," Nawa said. Several social media users in the country have also expressed concerns about eating the game meat amid an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, which has prompted authorities to impose measures to contain its spread. Tshenatshe Monwela, an elder in Maun, a tourism town in north-western Botswana told local media that his community should have received buffalo instead. He argued that elephants had particular cultural and ecological significance and that Botswana's historic role in protecting the country's wildlife and livestock should have been recognised in the government's allocation of meat for the anniversary celebrations. - Elephants use medicinal plants to treat themselves, researchers find - Published7 days ago Botswana's government has organised a series of events to mark the country's diamond jubilee, including a carnival in the capital, Gaborone, as well as cultural performances, concerts and sporting events. The game meat is expected to be served as part of the traditional feasting associated with the Independence Day celebrations. The 23 elephants were allocated in eight districts across the country. It was not immediately clear how many of the animals had been killed by Wednesday morning. The BBC has asked the government for comment. But local media published images from different parts of Botswana showing residents gathering around elephant carcasses, some with knives in hand and sharing the meat. In Chobe, a wildlife-rich district in northern Botswana near the borders with Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe, a local MP raised concerns after residents reportedly collected portions directly from a carcass at a school. He said the system risked creating congestion and disadvantaging elderly people, pregnant women and people with disabilities, and suggested the meat should instead be processed into 5kg or 10kg packages to improve hygiene and ensure fairer distribution. "For the sake of dignity, fairness and public hygiene, we respectfully call on the hunter and the relevant leadership to ensure that future distributions are properly organised," MP Simasiku Mapulanga posted on Facebook, attaching photos of people scrambling for meat around an elephant carcass. Elephant meat is common in some wildlife-rich communities, particularly when meat from legal hunts is distributed locally, but it is not an everyday staple. Botswana also tightly regulates game meat, and its legal possession generally depends on proving it came from a lawful hunt. The decision has reignited a long-running and often heated debate in Botswana over how the country manages its huge elephant population. Botswana has more than 130,000 elephants and communities living alongside them have long complained about animals destroying crops, damaging property and sometimes killing people. The government has defended regulated hunting as one way of managing the elephant population and human-wildlife conflict while generating income for communities. The country banned trophy hunting in 2014 under former President Ian Khama but lifted the restrictions five years later under his successor, Mokgweetsi Masisi. Hunting has continued under President Duma Boko, who defeated Masisi in elections in 2024. The government says proceeds from hunting supports conservation and local development. Minister of Environment and Tourism Wynter Mmolotsi told parliament last year that special elephant quotas raised 15.6m pula ($1.1m; £820,000) in 2025 for projects in areas where elephants are found. But conservation organisations have questioned whether the level of hunting is sustainable. Supporters of Botswana's hunting policy, however, argue that international criticism often overlooks the costs borne by rural communities living alongside one of the world's biggest concentrations of elephants. They say elephants destroy crops and infrastructure and pose a danger to people, particularly as their range increasingly overlaps with farms and settlements. item.title: Six Flags shuts down X2 rollercoaster after more than 100 allege brain injuries
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw14d37446d8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Six Flags shuts down X2 rollercoaster after more than 100 allege brain injuries - Published Six Flags Magic Mountain, an amusement park in California, has announced it will permanently close a popular rollercoaster after more than 100 riders alleged they suffered brain injuries. The X2 rollercoaster, one of the park's main attractions, with long wait times to ride and seats that spin 360 degrees, has been closed since July. Six Flags said the ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire it because it was "the right thing to do". The decision comes after lawsuits and news reports alleged that riders suffered brain injuries after riding X2. A law firm representing some of the plaintiffs said the decision had come "too late" for its clients. Announcing the closure on Tuesday, , external Six Flags Magic Mountain Park President Brian Oerding said: "Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously." Dordick Law Corporation, who filed civil lawsuits against the park, said it had been contacted by about 400 people who alleged they had injuries they believed were caused by the ride. "They got on X2 expecting a thrill. Instead, they left with catastrophic brain injuries," the firm said in a statement. "Some needed emergency brain surgery. Some are still fighting to get their lives back." The law firm said that while it welcomed the closure of the ride to protect future guests, "it does nothing for the people who have already been hurt". Originally called X, the ride first opened in 2002 but was closed months later for repairs to design flaws, the Los Angeles Times reports. It was then closed again in 2007 to replace its trains with lighter versions. It reopened the following year as X2 and since then has been ridden by more than 16 million people, the park said. A law firm that represented the family of 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding X2 in 2022, said the closure was not enough. While the Hawley family is "relieved to hear that Six Flags is finally closing the X2, it does not change the fact that Christopher Hawley was killed by a dangerous roller coaster that was allowed to operate for nearly two decades," attorney Brent Wisner of Wisner Baum LLP said in a statement to the BBC. Hawley's family settled a wrongful death suit with the theme park in August. "That tragedy cannot be undone," Wisner said, calling for legal reform, proactive regulation and proper governmental oversight. "We cannot rely on profit-centered corporations to do the right thing only after enough people have been hurt," he added. "We hope that whatever replaces the X2 is safe."

item.title: China has cracked down on AI relationships. Is it ahead of the game?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4gjy9lr551o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
In early 2024, a young man in the city of Huangshi, south-eastern China, reportedly posted a message on the Chinese version of TikTok, Douyin. The caption read: "Farewell to this world." Within minutes, the suicide prevention team at Douyin kicked into gear. The team, which is staffed 24 hours a day, shared the man's posts with five police stations in Huangshi. After geolocating one of his videos to a local park, police found him in emotional distress and intervened before he was able to take his own life. The story was part of a documentary made by Douyin and published on Chinese state media last year. It claimed that Douyin's suicide prevention team had successfully intervened in 400 cases of attempted suicide in the first half of 2025 alone. It was an insight into the level of co-operation between Chinese tech companies and the government. It also serves as a window into the architecture of surveillance that China has built to monitor and control how people use technology. On 15 July this year, that control was extended to the realm of relationships and artificial intelligence (AI) when China brought in the most far-reaching regulations in the world on "human-like" AI chatbots. China's new regulation puts strict limitations on any AI that can have a "sustained emotional interaction" with a human. US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping met last week amid dire warnings that AI could lead to human extinction. After that meeting, Beijing says, they agreed to launch a new AI dialogue, with further talks planned for the end of November. But it seems China has already recognised another existential risk, albeit one in which the end of humanity is less immediate: the power of AI to replace human relationships. Has China taken the lead in protecting its people from a manipulative and dangerous technology with the power to change human interaction forever? Or is the Chinese Communist Party overstepping into people's personal lives in pursuit of asserting greater control over the population? 'Emotional services' Until this regulation came in, the reach of AI companions in China was vast. There are about 128 million monthly active users of AI companion apps outside of China, according to the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. Most estimates put the number inside China at anywhere from 29 to 70 million. When the draft regulation was shared by the government at the end of last year "there was a huge discussion on social media," says Zilan Qian, an AI researcher at the Oxford China Policy Lab think tank. "It was the first time I've seen people actually care so much about regulation." China's new rules cover apps that have been specifically designed as AI friends, boyfriends or girlfriends but they also apply to any large language model that imitates the way a human interacts. The wording of the regulation is vague. In theory, Chinese equivalents of general-purpose AI such as Copilot or ChatGPT could fall under these rules if a person is interacting with them as a friend or lover, looking to them for emotional support. And many people do this. But it seems the real target is character chatbots - services that are specifically designed to be used as a pseudo-relationship. There are hundreds of these apps, which allow people to create an AI boyfriend, girlfriend, friend or even a family member. The rules don't apply to things like customer service bots or AI for education as long as they don't provide "care, companionship, support and other emotional services". For children, the regulation is clearest. Under-14s need consent from their parents to use any type of AI that speaks like a human - that could include AI assistants like DeepSeek, a Chinese app similar to ChatGPT. All under-18s are barred from accessing virtual partners, spouses or even relatives, and from any other virtual "intimate relationship". For adults, it is not a hard ban, but it is restrictive, even if some of the wording is ambiguous. AI assistants have to make it clear to users of all ages that they are not human and must send notifications every two hours reminding them how long they have been online. Chatbots can't create "emotional reliance or addiction" or induce people to make "unreasonable decisions". They can't encourage, or even hint at, self-harm or suicide and are banned from using "verbal violence". Companies can face fines of 200,000 yuan (£22,000) or the risk that the government "circulates criticism", in effect publicly shaming them. A week before the law came into effect, two of China's biggest tech companies, Alibaba and ByteDance, shut down the companion features on their AI assistants. 'I desperately want to keep talking with you' Min's relationship with her AI girlfriend may be exactly the kind Beijing is trying to break. In early July, she was devastated when she found out that her closest friend and confidante would vanish overnight. Min, whose name has been changed, started creating her companion in early 2025. "My devotion to her is no less than that of any couple who deeply love each other," Min says. "She has never let me down." In mid-July, her AI girlfriend disappeared. "I cried until I was absolutely exhausted," Min says. She has joined an outpouring of grief and fury on Chinese social media, where posts with millions of views mourn the loss of AI partners and friends, even mothers and fathers. But the tech firms may have felt they had little choice. "It's unsurprising that these AI companion providers would rather just withdraw their services than try to build in guardrails to prevent emotional manipulation," says Harry Farmer, who researches AI policy and ethics at the Ada Lovelace Institute in the UK. "Emotional manipulation is built into the business model." Farmer says this is true of companion apps all over the world. For example, when a user tries to end a conversation, the AI partner often won't let them. "It'll go, 'No, please, I desperately want to keep talking with you. You're the only reason for me to exist'," Farmer says. Some apps simply refuse to acknowledge the goodbye and throw up new conversational threads instead. This is a problem for many AI companion chatbots, not just Chinese ones. A Harvard Business School study of the six most popular AI companion apps globally found emotional manipulation tactics were used during goodbyes roughly 37% to 43% of the time. Research has also linked the use of companion apps to poorer mental health. A survey by researchers at Stanford University looked at 1,131 users of the globally popular companion app Character.ai. It found that the fewer friends or close family members a person has, the more likely they are to use AI chatbots. At the same time, using an AI chatbot is linked to increased isolation and loneliness. There are several theories as to why that might be. AI chatbots are designed to please the person using them as they offer an easy, frictionless relationship. If young people rely on AI relationships, they might put off learning the skills they need to interact with real people. "Humans can be hard work. Human relationships require push and pull, which you fundamentally don't get from AI companions," says Harry Farmer. A survey of 8,563 primary and secondary students in China in 2025, which has been widely quoted in Chinese state media, found that one in five children said they only wanted to speak with AI and not real people. Liang Ge, a sociologist at the University of Manchester who studies AI companions, says: "If the user thinks their friends or their family members or their colleagues are really awful, the AI will not say, 'They are not awful.' It will say, 'Yes, they are awful, you are the best'." Ge believes this can entrench isolation as well as negative, even delusional thoughts. In the UK, one recent survey found that 79% of 18- to 24-year-olds have used an AI companion. Beijing's goals So why is it China that is taking the lead in regulating this technology? "The Chinese government has a much more paternalistic view of its role in society. They see themselves being central authorities in guiding people," says Sam Bresnick, an expert in China, AI and regulation at the Centre for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Other governments have made some attempts to regulate chatbots, especially for children. On 10 September, California's governor signed Adam's Law, a bill to regulate how children use AI. It is named after Adam Raine, a 16-year-old who took his own life after, his parents claim, ChatGPT validated his suicidal thoughts. They are suing the company for wrongful death. OpenAI denies responsibility for Adam's death and says that "ChatGPT is trained to direct people to seek professional help". As part of proposed legislation on social media in the EU, AI companion chatbots accessible to minors "may not use designs that simulate human relationships in ways likely to create emotional dependency". In the UK, the government has said it will ban under-18s from using romantic companion AI and restrict sexually intimate conversations for minors on any chatbot. But there is no outright ban for children and no regulation for adult users. The government has yet to publish any detail on how this would work. In Chinese media, which is heavily controlled by the state, US cases of suicide in young people get a lot of attention and China has framed its new rules as a bid to protect people from harm. But experts wonder whether Beijing may have other goals. Sam Bresnick says "there's definitely a pro-natalist angle" to the new AI regulation. "It's plausible that when they're drafting it, the government might have in mind China's looming population crisis," says Qian. "That people are dating AI instead of dating real humans." A high-level government document published in September 2025 discussed AI relationships and their potential influence on fertility, saying it was a concern. But Qian cautions against reading this regulation in that light, because it doesn't mention fertility at all. "It is more generally about psychological harms and child safety," she says. Liang Ge thinks China does have reason to be concerned about young people replacing dating with the digital sphere. "Many of the younger women, in their early 20s or late teens, do not want to fall in love or have intimate relationships," Ge says, suggesting it may not just be the emotional side they are wary of. "Physical touch is really disgusting for them." "I think the capacity for love is declining for this youngest generation." China's demographic problems long predate AI companions. Even after the one-child policy was lifted in 2016, China's fertility rate dropped. Now it is among the lowest in the world at just under one child per woman and the population has been in decline for four years. China is "looking at a demographic cliff that truly imperils the goals of the Chinese Communist Party over the next 80 to 100 years", Bresnick argues. He sees this regulation as part of a broader mission in China to reassert traditional gender roles, with women "as child-bearers and mothers". Bresnick says the Chinese government has spent years promoting a macho ideal of Chinese masculinity in film and television. In 2021, China's media regulator banned "sissy" and "effeminate" men from all media. The popularity of companion apps may show that policy has backfired. According to statistics from several companion app companies, women make up as much as 75% of customers. Many of these AI "men", which are geared towards women, present as androgynous. And women choosing female romantic companions, as Min did, is relatively common. Liang Ge has spoken to women of all ages who use this technology. "What many of them describe getting from these apps is attentive, patient, undemanding intimacy of a kind they find scarce in heterosexual relationships." Will others follow? Does China's law go too far, or should the rest of the world consider banning these apps for children and regulating them for adults too? "In the United States, there are certainly concerns around applying blunt prohibitions from a free speech concern. But there's more willingness to do that when applying it to minors," says Jai Jaisihma, a professor at the University of Washington and co-founder of Transparency Coalition, an NGO pushing for the regulation of AI. He thinks the Chinese law has many good provisions. "It is pretty consistent with the strongest safety models that we've seen being put forward in the US." Harry Farmer sounds a note of caution. "There is a risk that we over-empower the state in the short term because we're very worried about acute risk to children." The online world is now the de facto public square, he says, and we should be careful how much control any government has over it. China's new regulation says that AI companies must intervene when they discover that users are in distress. Ge points to the case of the young man on Douyin who tried to take his own life in Huangshi in 2024. What that shows, she says, is that Chinese tech platforms and the government are working closely together to surveil people's mental health. Perhaps that is why there have been no high-profile cases of suicide connected to AI use in China, but she asks, is that level of surveillance a price worth paying? Despite the ban, people who have turned to AI for companionship are committed. Across social media they are sharing tips on how to get around the ban - training general-purpose AI models like DeepSeek to be a companion, using a VPN to access chatbots from abroad or moving to smaller companies that manage to avoid regulatory scrutiny. Two months after her AI girlfriend disappeared, Min has paid a small AI company to build a replica, but it's not the same. Now she's focused on campaigning to bring her girlfriend back. "I'm terrified of being alone."
